specStatements.text: There are two ways of joining electrical components, in series and in parallel. Some circuits include both series and parallel parts.
• there is the same current through each component
• the total potential difference of the power supply is shared between the components
• the total resistance of two components is the sum of the resistance of each component.
• the potential difference across each component is the same
• the total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components
• the total resistance of two resistors is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.
• use circuit diagrams to construct and check series and parallel circuits that include a variety of common circuit components
• describe the difference between series and parallel circuits
• explain qualitatively why adding resistors in series increases the total resistance whilst adding resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance
• explain the design and use of dc series circuits for measurement and testing purposes
• calculate the currents, potential differences and resistances in dc series circuits
• solve problems for circuits which include resistors in series using the concept of equivalent resistance.
Students are not required to calculate the total resistance of two resistors joined in parallel.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not required to calculate the total resistance of two resistors joined in parallel.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No reciprocal formula (1/R_total = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2) and no product-over-sum shortcut appears anywhere in this content, and no item asks for a numerical value of the combined resistance of a parallel pair. Parallel resistance is treated only as the qualitative statement the specification does require: the total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor, explained by the extra path the second resistor offers. Where numbers appear alongside a parallel pair (q08) the student judges only whether a value is possible, using the 'less than the smallest' rule, which needs no calculation. Every calculation item (q03, q07, q14, q15, q16) is confined to dc series circuits or to adding branch currents, both of which the specification does require.

concepts.definition: Components are in series when they are joined one after another in a single loop, so there is only one path for charge. Every charge that passes through one component must pass through all the others.
Components are in parallel when they are joined side by side between the same two points, so the charge has a choice of paths. Each component sits on its own branch of the circuit.
A point in a circuit where the conducting path divides or rejoins. Charge that arrives at a junction each second equals the charge that leaves it each second, so no charge is created or lost there.
In series there is the same current through each component, because there is only one path and charge is not used up. Moving an ammeter to a different place in the loop does not change its reading.

concepts.term: Sharing of potential difference in series
concepts.definition: The total potential difference of the power supply is shared between components connected in series, so the separate potential differences add up to the supply potential difference.
The total resistance of two components in series is the sum of the resistance of each component, R_total = R_1 + R_2, because the charge has to pass through both in turn.
The potential difference across each component connected in parallel is the same, because the ends of every branch are joined to the same two points in the circuit.

concepts.term: Total current in a parallel circuit
concepts.definition: The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components, because the current from the supply divides between the branches and rejoins afterwards.
The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor, because the second resistor gives the charge an extra path to flow along.
The unit of resistance, R, is the ohm, symbol Ω. A component has a resistance of one ohm when a potential difference of one volt across it drives a current of one ampere through it.
A single resistance that could replace a group of resistors without changing the current drawn from the supply. For resistors in series it is found by adding the individual resistances.
An ammeter measures current and is connected in series with the component whose current is wanted, so that the same current passes through both the meter and that component.
A voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel with the component, that is across its two ends, so it experiences the same potential difference as that component.
A direct current supply, such as a cell or battery, drives charge around the circuit in one direction only. The dc series circuits used for measurement and testing are built from such a supply.
A circuit that contains both series and parallel parts, for example a resistor in series with a pair of lamps that are in parallel with each other.

concepts.term: Variable resistor in a test circuit
concepts.definition: A resistor whose resistance can be changed. Placed in series in a test circuit it alters the current, so several pairs of current and potential difference readings can be taken for one component.

misconceptions.question: In a series circuit one ammeter is placed before a lamp and a second after it. How do the readings compare?
misconceptions.correct: Both ammeters give the same reading, because there is the same current through each component in series.
misconceptions.misconception: The current is used up in the lamp, so the ammeter after the lamp reads less than the one before it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear that a lamp 'uses' electricity and transfer that to the current rather than to the energy carried by the charge.
misconceptions.correction: Charge is not used up: the charge that enters a component leaves it again. What is transferred is energy, shown by the potential difference across the lamp, not the current.

misconceptions.question: Two components are in series with a cell. Is the current from the cell divided between them?
misconceptions.correct: No. In series the same current passes through both components; it is the potential difference that is shared.
misconceptions.misconception: The current from the cell splits between the two components, so each gets half of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'shared' is remembered from the potential difference rule and applied to current instead.
misconceptions.correction: Current only divides where the path divides, at a junction. A series loop has no junctions, so the same current is in every part of it.

misconceptions.question: A 6 V supply is in series with two identical lamps. What is the potential difference across one lamp?
misconceptions.correct: 3 V. The total potential difference of the supply is shared between the components in series.
misconceptions.misconception: 6 V. Each component in series has the full potential difference of the supply across it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The parallel rule, that the potential difference across each component is the same, is applied to a series circuit.
misconceptions.correction: Full supply potential difference across each component is the parallel rule. In series the separate potential differences add up to the supply value.

misconceptions.question: A 20 Ω and a 5 Ω resistor are joined in parallel. What can be said about the total resistance?
misconceptions.correct: It is less than 5 Ω, because the total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the smallest individual resistance.
misconceptions.misconception: It is 25 Ω, because the two resistances are added together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: R_total = R_1 + R_2 is memorised as the rule for all combinations, without noticing that it is stated only for series.
misconceptions.correction: Adding applies to series only. In parallel the extra branch gives charge another route, so the pair opposes the current less than either resistor alone.

misconceptions.question: Why does adding a resistor in series increase the total resistance?
misconceptions.correct: The charge has to pass through both resistors in turn, so there is more opposition along the single path.
misconceptions.misconception: Adding a second resistor in series just gives the charge another path to follow, like a parallel branch, so the total resistance falls.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'extra path' picture belongs to parallel connection and is attached to the series case as well.
misconceptions.correction: An extra series resistor lengthens the one path; an extra parallel resistor adds a new path. More path raises resistance, more paths lowers it.

misconceptions.question: Two branches of a parallel circuit carry 0.40 A and 0.25 A. What is the supply current?
misconceptions.correct: 0.65 A. The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components.
misconceptions.misconception: 0.40 A, because the current is the same everywhere in any circuit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The series rule 'same current through each component' is generalised to every circuit, including parallel ones.
misconceptions.correction: The same-current rule applies along one path. Where the path divides, the branch currents add to give the total current in the main part of the circuit.

misconceptions.question: Two lamps are in parallel across a 12 V battery. What is the potential difference across each lamp?
misconceptions.correct: 12 V across each lamp, because the potential difference across each component in parallel is the same.
misconceptions.misconception: 6 V across each lamp, because the battery potential difference is shared between the two branches.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The sharing rule for series is carried over to parallel, since two components again have to 'divide' something.
misconceptions.correction: In parallel it is the current that divides, not the potential difference. Each branch is connected to the same two points, so each has the full supply potential difference.

misconceptions.question: How should an ammeter and a voltmeter be connected to test one lamp?
misconceptions.correct: The ammeter goes in series with the lamp and the voltmeter in parallel with it, across its two ends.
misconceptions.misconception: The ammeter goes across the lamp and the voltmeter is placed in the main loop with it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both meters are seen simply as things to add to the circuit, without linking the connection to the quantity being measured.
misconceptions.correction: A meter must experience the quantity it reads: the ammeter must carry the lamp's current, so it is in series, and the voltmeter must span the lamp's ends, so it is in parallel.

misconceptions.question: A 9 V supply is in series with a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor. How is the potential difference shared?
misconceptions.correct: 3 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 6 V across the 4 Ω resistor, since the same current passes through both.
misconceptions.misconception: 4.5 V across each, because the supply potential difference is always split equally between the components.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Shared' is read as 'shared equally', ignoring the different resistances of the components.
misconceptions.correction: The share depends on resistance. With the same current in both, the larger resistance takes the larger potential difference; the two shares still add to 9 V.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter where in a series loop a component is placed relative to the cell?
misconceptions.correct: No. The current is the same through every component, whatever the order of components in the loop.
misconceptions.misconception: The component nearest the cell takes more current, leaving less for the ones further round the loop.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge is pictured as a supply of stuff that is handed out along the way, so the first component gets first choice.
misconceptions.correction: Current is not handed out along a series loop. The same current passes through every component, so swapping their order changes none of the readings.

misconceptions.question: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are joined in series. What is the total resistance?
misconceptions.correct: 10 Ω, because the total resistance of two components in series is the sum of the resistance of each component.
misconceptions.misconception: 2 Ω, found by taking the difference between the two resistance values.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Combining two numbers is remembered as a vague instruction, and subtraction is chosen once the answer 'feels' as if it should be smaller.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives R_total = R_1 + R_2 for series. Resistances in series add, so the total is always larger than either separate resistance.

misconceptions.question: Two lamps are in parallel and one is removed. What happens to the other lamp?
misconceptions.correct: It stays lit at the same brightness, because it still has the full supply potential difference across its own branch.
misconceptions.misconception: It becomes brighter, because it now receives all of the current that the two lamps used to share.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The supply is imagined to deliver a fixed amount of current that is divided up, rather than a current set by the resistance of each branch.
misconceptions.correction: The current in a branch is set by its own resistance and the potential difference across it. Neither changes when the other branch is removed, so the brightness is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: What quantity, symbol and unit are used for resistance?
misconceptions.correct: Resistance, symbol R, measured in ohms, unit symbol Ω, exactly as the specification states.
misconceptions.misconception: Resistance is given the symbol Ω and measured in units called R.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The quantity symbol and the unit symbol are learnt as a pair without noting which is which.
misconceptions.correction: R is the quantity symbol used in equations such as R_total = R_1 + R_2; Ω is the symbol for the unit, the ohm, that the value is measured in.

misconceptions.question: Three 6 Ω resistors are in series. What single resistance could replace them?
misconceptions.correct: 18 Ω, the equivalent resistance found by adding all three resistances.
misconceptions.misconception: 6 Ω, because the largest resistor controls the circuit and the others make no difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The idea that the biggest resistance is the bottleneck is borrowed from everyday reasoning about narrow gaps.
misconceptions.correction: Every series resistor adds its own opposition, so all of them count. The equivalent resistance is the sum, here 6 Ω + 6 Ω + 6 Ω = 18 Ω.

misconceptions.question: A voltmeter across the second of two series lamps reads what, if the first already reads 3 V of a 6 V supply?
misconceptions.correct: 3 V, because the two shares of the supply potential difference add up to 6 V.
misconceptions.misconception: 0 V or nearly nothing, because the first lamp has already used up the potential difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Potential difference is treated as a fuel carried round the loop and spent at the first component reached.
misconceptions.correction: Potential difference is not a store that runs out along the way; it is a measure of energy transferred per unit charge at each component. The shares add to the supply value.

misconceptions.question: Do two parallel lamps have the same potential difference only if they are identical?
misconceptions.correct: No. The potential difference across each component in parallel is the same whatever their resistances are.
misconceptions.misconception: They only have equal potential differences when the two lamps have the same resistance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Symmetry is thought to be doing the work, so the rule is believed to fail when the branches differ.
misconceptions.correction: The rule follows from the connection, not from the components: both branches end on the same two points, so both have the same potential difference across them.

misconceptions.question: A 20 Ω and a 5 Ω resistor are in parallel. Where does the total resistance lie?
misconceptions.correct: Below 5 Ω, since the total resistance of the pair is less than the smallest individual resistance.
misconceptions.misconception: Between 5 Ω and 20 Ω, because a combined value must lie somewhere between the two.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Averaging is assumed to be the safe answer whenever two values are combined.
misconceptions.correction: Adding a parallel branch always makes it easier for charge to flow, so the total falls below even the smallest of the individual resistances.

misconceptions.question: What does the variable resistor do in a dc series test circuit?
misconceptions.correct: It changes the current in the circuit, so several pairs of readings can be taken for the component under test.
misconceptions.misconception: It holds the current steady while the potential difference across the component is changed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The variable resistor is remembered as a control, and 'control' is read as 'keep constant'.
misconceptions.correction: Changing its resistance changes the total resistance of the series loop and so changes the current, which is exactly what is wanted to build up a set of readings.

misconceptions.question: Is the variable resistor needed to make the current the same in every part of a series circuit?
misconceptions.correct: No. The current is already the same through each component in series, whatever the variable resistor is set to.
misconceptions.misconception: The variable resistor is there to even out the current so that every component gets the same amount.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A job is invented for the component from a property of series circuits that is true for a different reason.
misconceptions.correction: Equal current in series follows from there being one path. The variable resistor is added to alter the size of that current, not to make it equal.

misconceptions.question: Must a circuit be either entirely in series or entirely in parallel?
misconceptions.correct: No. Some circuits include both series and parallel parts, such as a resistor in series with two parallel lamps.
misconceptions.misconception: Every circuit is either a series circuit or a parallel circuit, so it must be labelled as one of the two.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two arrangements are first met as opposites, and the pair is taken to be a complete set of choices.
misconceptions.correction: Series and parallel describe how any two components are joined, not the whole circuit. Many circuits contain both kinds of connection at once.

misconceptions.question: A 12 V supply is in series with a 3 Ω and a 5 Ω resistor. What is the current?
misconceptions.correct: 1.5 A, because the current is the supply potential difference divided by the total resistance of 8 Ω.
misconceptions.misconception: 4 A, because the current is worked out from the supply and one of the resistors on its own.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The resistor being looked at is used in the calculation while the rest of the series loop is forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: The current is set by the whole loop. Add the resistances first to get the total, here 8 Ω, then divide the supply potential difference by that total.

misconceptions.question: In what unit is resistance measured?
misconceptions.correct: In ohms, unit symbol Ω, as the specification states: resistance, R, in ohms, Ω.
misconceptions.misconception: Resistance is measured in volts, because a voltmeter is used when resistance is investigated.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three electrical quantities are met together, and the unit of the one that is easiest to picture is attached to all of them.
misconceptions.correction: The volt is the unit of potential difference and the ampere the unit of current. Resistance has its own unit, the ohm, symbol Ω.

misconceptions.question: Two branches carry 0.40 A and 0.25 A. How are these combined to give the supply current?
misconceptions.correct: They are added, giving 0.65 A, because the total current is the sum of the currents through the separate components.
misconceptions.misconception: They are subtracted, or averaged, to give the current in the main part of the circuit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any pair of numbers is combined by whichever operation gives a value that looks reasonable, rather than by thinking about charge at a junction.
misconceptions.correction: Charge is conserved at a junction: everything that flows in along the branches flows out along the main wire, so the branch currents add.

misconceptions.question: Three lamps are in series and one is removed. What happens to the other two?
misconceptions.correct: They go out, because there is only one path and removing a component breaks it.
misconceptions.misconception: They stay lit, because each lamp still has its own path back to the cell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The independence of parallel branches is remembered as a general fact about circuits with several lamps.
misconceptions.correction: Only parallel branches are independent. A series circuit is a single loop, so a gap anywhere stops the current everywhere.

misconceptions.question: Two lamps are in parallel and one is removed. What happens to the other?
misconceptions.correct: It stays lit as before, because its own branch is still a complete path with the full supply across it.
misconceptions.misconception: It goes out, because removing a lamp breaks the circuit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The series result is applied to every circuit, since removing a lamp is pictured as making a gap in one shared loop.
misconceptions.correction: In parallel each branch is a complete path on its own. Breaking one branch leaves the other branch, and its potential difference, unchanged.

misconceptions.question: A student wants to measure both the current in a lamp and the potential difference across it. Can both meters simply be wired into the main circuit loop with the lamp?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the ammeter goes in series in the loop. The voltmeter must be connected in parallel, across the two ends of the lamp, because potential difference is a difference between two points.
misconceptions.misconception: Meters are just extra components you slot into the circuit, so both the ammeter and the voltmeter go in series in the loop, one on each side of the lamp.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students build circuits by adding each new part into the single loop, and they generalise this habit to every device, not realising a voltmeter measures a difference between two points rather than something flowing through it.
misconceptions.correction: An ammeter measures the current through a component, so it sits in series in the same loop. A voltmeter measures the potential difference between the two ends of a component, so its two leads must touch those two ends: it is connected in parallel. A voltmeter placed in series has a very high resistance and would almost stop the current.

misconceptions.question: A student wants to measure the current in a lamp and the potential difference across it. Should both meters be connected across the ends of the lamp?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the voltmeter goes across the lamp. The ammeter must be placed in series in the loop, so that the current through the lamp also passes through it.
misconceptions.misconception: A meter reads a component by being connected across it, so both the ammeter and the voltmeter are clipped across the two ends of the lamp.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see voltmeters and multimeter probes touched across components and conclude that 'across the ends' is how all measuring instruments work, without thinking about what each meter actually measures.
misconceptions.correction: An ammeter measures current, the flow of charge through the lamp, so the same current must flow through the ammeter: it goes in series. Only the voltmeter, which compares the potential at the two ends, is connected in parallel. An ammeter in parallel has a very low resistance and would short-circuit the lamp.

mcqs.stem: A lamp and a fixed resistor are connected in series with a cell. An ammeter placed between the cell and the lamp reads 0.30 A. A second ammeter is placed between the lamp and the resistor. What does the second ammeter read?

options.text: Less than 0.30 A, because some of the current is used up inside the lamp
options.rationale: A student who thinks current is consumed expects the reading after the lamp to have fallen.

options.text: 0.15 A, because the current from the cell is shared between the two parts
options.rationale: The sharing rule, which applies to potential difference, is wrongly applied to the current.

options.text: 0.30 A, because in series there is the same current through each of the components
options.rationale: For components connected in series there is the same current through each component, so both ammeters read 0.30 A.

options.text: 0.30 A, but only if the resistor is placed nearer to the cell than the lamp
options.rationale: Order in a series loop is thought to matter, as if the first component took a larger share.

mcqs.stem: A 6 V battery is connected in series with two identical lamps. A voltmeter across the first lamp reads 3 V. What does a voltmeter across the second lamp read?

options.text: 3 V, because the supply potential difference is shared between the two lamps
options.rationale: The total potential difference of the power supply is shared between components in series, so the two equal shares are 3 V each.

options.text: 6 V, because each component in series has the full supply potential difference
options.rationale: The parallel rule that each component has the same potential difference is applied to a series circuit.

options.text: 0 V, because the first lamp has already used up the potential difference
options.rationale: Potential difference is imagined as a fuel spent at the first component the charge reaches.

options.text: 3 V, but only if the second lamp is the one nearer to the negative terminal
options.rationale: Position in the loop is treated as important, when identical lamps share equally wherever they sit.

mcqs.stem: A 4 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are joined in series. What is the total resistance of the pair?

options.text: 2 Ω, found by taking the difference of the two values
options.rationale: The two numbers are combined by subtraction rather than by the addition the specification gives.

options.text: 5 Ω, the value that lies midway between the two resistors
options.rationale: Averaging is chosen as a safe way to combine two numbers, but series resistances add.

options.text: Under 4 Ω, since joining resistors gives the charge more paths
options.rationale: The parallel picture of an extra path is applied to a series pair, which has only one path.

options.text: 10 Ω, found by adding the two resistance values together
options.rationale: R_total = R_1 + R_2, so the total resistance is 4 Ω + 6 Ω = 10 Ω.

mcqs.stem: The specification gives the equation R_total = R_1 + R_2. Which statement does this equation express?

options.text: The total resistance of two components in parallel is the sum of each resistance
options.rationale: The series addition rule is applied to parallel resistors, where the total is instead below the smallest.

options.text: The total resistance of two components in series is the sum of each resistance
options.rationale: This is the series rule exactly as the specification states it: the total resistance of two components is the sum of the resistance of each component.

options.text: The total resistance of two components in series is set by the larger resistor alone
options.rationale: The larger resistor is treated as a bottleneck that decides the total on its own.

options.text: The total resistance of two components in series lies midway between the two values
options.rationale: Combining is read as averaging, which would make the total smaller than one of the resistors.

mcqs.stem: A student is writing a key for a circuit table. Which line gives the quantity, its symbol and its unit for resistance as the specification states them?

options.text: Resistance, symbol Ω, measured in units called R, put after the value
options.rationale: The quantity symbol and the unit symbol have been swapped over.

options.text: Resistance, symbol R, measured in volts, whose unit symbol is V
options.rationale: The unit of potential difference is attached to resistance, a common mix-up between the two quantities.

options.text: Resistance, symbol I, measured in ohms, whose unit symbol is Ω
options.rationale: I is the symbol for current, not resistance, though the unit given here is right.

options.text: Resistance, symbol R, measured in ohms, for which the unit symbol is Ω
options.rationale: The specification states: resistance, R, in ohms, Ω.

mcqs.stem: Two lamps of different resistances are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. A voltmeter across the first lamp reads 12 V. What does a voltmeter across the second lamp read?

options.text: 6 V, since the potential difference of the battery is shared between the two branches
options.rationale: The series sharing rule is applied to a parallel circuit, where the potential difference is not divided.

options.text: Less than 12 V, since the first lamp has taken some potential difference
options.rationale: Potential difference is treated as something used up on the way round the circuit.

options.text: 12 V, since the potential difference across each component in parallel is the same
options.rationale: Both branches are joined between the same two points, so each has the full 12 V across it.

options.text: 12 V, but only when both of the lamps have exactly the same resistance
options.rationale: The rule is thought to depend on the branches matching, when it follows only from how they are joined.

mcqs.stem: In a parallel circuit one branch carries a current of 0.40 A and the other carries 0.25 A. What is the current in the wire leading from the supply?

options.text: 0.65 A, the sum of the currents in the two branches
options.rationale: The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components.

options.text: 0.40 A, the same as the current within the larger branch
options.rationale: The series rule of one current everywhere is applied to a circuit whose path divides.

options.text: 0.15 A, found from the difference of the branch values
options.rationale: The branch values are subtracted, which would mean charge disappearing at the junction.

options.text: 0.325 A, the average of the two branch currents
options.rationale: Averaging is used to combine the two readings, but currents entering a junction add.

mcqs.stem: A 20 Ω resistor and a 5 Ω resistor are joined in parallel. Which statement about the total resistance of this pair is correct?

options.text: It is 25 Ω, the two resistance values added together
options.rationale: The series addition rule has been applied to a parallel pair.

options.text: It is below 5 Ω, the smaller of the two resistances
options.rationale: The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.

options.text: It is 12.5 Ω, halfway between the two resistance values
options.rationale: Averaging is used, which also wrongly puts the total above the smaller resistor.

options.text: It is between 5 Ω and 20 Ω, but closer to the 5 Ω one
options.rationale: The total is assumed to lie between the two values, when it must fall below both of them.

mcqs.stem: Explain why connecting a second resistor in series with the first increases the total resistance of the circuit.

options.text: The charge now has to pass through both resistors in turn, so the single path opposes it more
options.rationale: In series the one path is effectively made harder to get through, so the resistances add and the total rises.

options.text: The second resistor gives the charge another path to follow, and each path opposes it
options.rationale: The extra path belongs to parallel connection; a series resistor extends the one path instead.

options.text: The second resistor uses up part of the current before it reaches the first resistor
options.rationale: Current is pictured as being consumed, rather than being the same through each series component.

options.text: The supply now has to share its potential difference, so it pushes the charge less hard
options.rationale: Sharing of potential difference is a consequence of the resistors, not the cause of the higher resistance.

mcqs.stem: Explain why connecting a second resistor in parallel with the first decreases the total resistance of the circuit.

options.text: The two resistance values simply add, and the supply is shared between the branches
options.rationale: Series addition is applied to a parallel pair, which would raise rather than lower the total.

options.text: The total has to lie between the two values, so it falls below the larger
options.rationale: A value between the two is still wrong: the parallel total is below even the smaller resistor.

options.text: The second resistor adds another path, so more charge can flow for the same supply
options.rationale: An extra route for charge means a larger total current for the same potential difference, which is a smaller total resistance.

options.text: Each of the resistors now carries only half the current, so each opposes it less
options.rationale: Resistance does not depend on the current in the component, and the branch currents need not be equal.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly describes a difference between series circuits and parallel circuits?

options.text: In series the potential difference is the same across each component; in parallel the current is
options.rationale: The two rules have been swapped between the two arrangements.

options.text: In series the components share out the current; in parallel they share the potential difference
options.rationale: Both halves are wrong: current is shared in parallel and potential difference is shared in series.

options.text: In series there is one path for charge; in parallel each branch carries equal current
options.rationale: The first half is right but branch currents are only equal when the branches have equal resistance.

options.text: In series the current is the same in each component; in parallel the potential difference is
options.rationale: This states both rules the specification gives: same current through each series component, same potential difference across each parallel component.

mcqs.stem: A student wants to measure the current in a lamp and the potential difference across it. How should the two meters be connected?

options.text: Ammeter in parallel with the lamp, voltmeter in series with it
options.rationale: The two connections have been exchanged, so neither meter measures the quantity it should.

options.text: Ammeter in series with the lamp, voltmeter across its ends
options.rationale: The ammeter must carry the lamp's current, so it goes in series; the voltmeter must span the lamp's ends, so it goes in parallel.

options.text: Both of the meters in series with the lamp, one on each side
options.rationale: A voltmeter in the loop cannot read the potential difference across the lamp alone.

options.text: Both of the meters in parallel with the lamp, across its ends
options.rationale: An ammeter across the lamp does not carry the lamp's current and would short it out.

mcqs.stem: A dc series circuit for testing a component contains a cell, an ammeter, a variable resistor and the component, with a voltmeter across the component. Why is the variable resistor included?

options.text: It keeps the current steady while the potential difference across the component is varied
options.rationale: A control is assumed to hold something constant; here it is used to change the current on purpose.

options.text: It makes the current the same in every part of the circuit while the test is carried out
options.rationale: Equal current in series already follows from there being a single path, so this is not its job.

options.text: It protects the voltmeter by taking a share of the current passing the meter
options.rationale: A voltmeter is connected across the component and is not in the path the variable resistor controls.

options.text: It changes the current, so several pairs of readings can be taken for the component under test
options.rationale: Altering its resistance alters the total resistance of the series loop, and so the current, giving a range of readings.

mcqs.stem: A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 3 Ω resistor and a 5 Ω resistor. What is the current in the circuit?

options.text: 1.5 A, from 12 V divided by the total resistance of 8 Ω
options.rationale: The series resistances add to 8 Ω, and 12 V ÷ 8 Ω = 1.5 A, the same current through both resistors.

options.text: 4 A, from 12 V divided by the 3 Ω resistor on its own
options.rationale: Only one resistor is used, so the opposition of the rest of the loop is ignored.

options.text: 6 A, from 12 V divided by the 2 Ω difference of the pair
options.rationale: The resistances are subtracted instead of added before the division is done.

options.text: 2.4 A, from 12 V divided by the 5 Ω resistor by itself
options.rationale: The larger resistor is treated as the only one that matters in the calculation.

mcqs.stem: A 9 V supply is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor?

options.text: 9 V, as each component has the whole supply across it
options.rationale: The parallel rule is applied, but in series the supply potential difference is shared.

options.text: 4.5 V, as the supply is shared equally between them
options.rationale: 'Shared' is read as 'shared equally', ignoring the different resistances.

options.text: 6 V, from the 1.5 A current in the 4 Ω resistor
options.rationale: Total resistance 6 Ω gives a current of 1.5 A, and 1.5 A × 4 Ω = 6 V across the larger resistor.

options.text: 3 V, an equal share among the three parts
options.rationale: Equal-split thinking (m10): the 9 V is divided equally across all three circuit parts, the cell and the two resistors, giving 3 V each.

mcqs.stem: Three 6 Ω resistors are connected in series across a 9 V supply. Using the idea of equivalent resistance, what current does the supply deliver?

options.text: 1.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of 6 Ω alone
options.rationale: Only the value of one resistor is used, as if the largest single resistance set the current.

options.text: 0.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of 18 Ω
options.rationale: The three series resistances add to an equivalent 18 Ω, and 9 V ÷ 18 Ω = 0.5 A.

options.text: 3 A, using an equivalent resistance of just 3 Ω
options.rationale: The total is assumed to fall as resistors are added, which is the behaviour of parallel resistors.

options.text: 4.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of just 2 Ω
options.rationale: 6 Ω has been divided by three rather than the three resistances being added together.

mcqs.stem: In a circuit a cell is joined to a resistor, and the resistor is joined to two lamps that are placed side by side between the same pair of junctions. How is this circuit best described?

options.text: It has both kinds of part: the resistor is in series with a parallel pair of lamps
options.rationale: Some circuits include both series and parallel parts, and this is one of them.

options.text: It is a series circuit, because all of the components are joined to one cell
options.rationale: Sharing a cell does not make components series; the two lamps sit between the same junctions.

options.text: It is a parallel circuit, because the circuit contains more than one branch
options.rationale: The presence of a branch does not make the resistor parallel to anything; it is in the main path.

options.text: It is neither, because a circuit has to be all series or all parallel
options.rationale: Series and parallel describe how components are joined, and a circuit may contain both.

mcqs.stem: Three lamps are connected in series with a cell. One lamp is taken out of its holder. What happens to the other two lamps?

options.text: They both stay lit, because each lamp has its own path back to the cell
options.rationale: Separate paths belong to a parallel circuit; a series loop offers only one.

options.text: They both stay lit but shine brighter, as the total resistance falls
options.rationale: Removing a series lamp does lower the resistance of the loop, but it also breaks the circuit.

options.text: They both go out, because the single path round the circuit has been broken
options.rationale: In series there is only one path, so removing any component stops the current everywhere in the loop.

options.text: The lamp before the empty holder stays lit, but the lamp after it goes out
options.rationale: Current is imagined to weaken along the path, but in series it is the same through each component.

mcqs.stem: Two lamps are connected in parallel across a cell. One of the lamps is taken out of its holder. What happens to the remaining lamp?

options.text: It goes out, since taking one lamp out breaks the circuit
options.rationale: This is the series behaviour; in parallel each branch is a complete path on its own.

options.text: It stays lit as before, since its own branch is still complete
options.rationale: The remaining branch still has the full supply potential difference across it, so its current is unchanged.

options.text: It shines more brightly, since it now receives all of the current
options.rationale: The supply current is not a fixed amount shared out; each branch current is set by its own branch.

options.text: It shines more dimly, since the supply now delivers less current
options.rationale: Less total current is drawn, but the current in the remaining branch itself does not change.

mcqs.stem: A circuit diagram shows a cell, a closed switch and two lamps drawn side by side between the same two junctions. Which measurement would best check that the built circuit matches the diagram?

options.text: Check that exactly the same current passes through each of the lamps
options.rationale: Equal branch currents happen only when the branches match, so this proves nothing about the connection.

options.text: Check that the two lamp potential differences add up to the supply value
options.rationale: Adding to the supply value is the series test, so this would show the build was wrong.

options.text: Check that the pair has a larger resistance than either lamp on its own
options.rationale: Series addition is used; a parallel pair has a resistance below that of the smaller lamp.

options.text: Check that each lamp has the full supply potential difference on it
options.rationale: Equal potential difference across each component, equal to the supply, is the test for a parallel connection.
